theme: The Gibeonite deception; the southern campaign
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 9:1-10:43. The first chapter is a story about deception and a hasty oath. The second is a story about a great victory in which God fights from heaven. Notice how the two are connected: the treaty with Gibeon is what pulls Israel into the southern campaign.
settingTheScene: After Ai, news of Israel’s victories has spread across the land. The kings of the hill country gather in an alliance to fight Joshua. But one group has another plan. The Gibeonites, a Hivite people living only a few miles away, decide to trick Israel into a peace treaty by pretending to come from a distant country. They put on worn-out clothing and carry moldy bread. Joshua and the leaders fall for it, and make a covenant with them without asking the LORD. The consequences of that oath will shape Israel’s history for centuries. Yet God uses even Israel’s mistake to bring about a remarkable day.
observation: The Gibeonites disguise themselves with old sacks, worn wineskins, patched sandals, and dry, moldy bread (9:4-5).
The Israelites “took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD” (9:14).
Joshua makes peace with them and the leaders swear an oath (9:15).
Three days later the deception is discovered, but the leaders refuse to break the oath: “We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel” (9:18-19).
The Gibeonites are made woodcutters and water carriers for the house of God (9:21-27).
Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and Joshua marches all night to rescue them (10:5-9).
The LORD threw large hailstones from heaven, and more died from the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword (10:11).
Joshua says, “Sun, stand still at Gibeon,” and the text records, “There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man” (10:12-14).
interpretation:
The Gibeonite story is a lesson in discernment. Israel has just seen God defeat Jericho and Ai, and they might be tempted to feel that they can handle anything. But the text records a single sentence that explains the problem: “they did not ask counsel from the LORD.” They looked at the bread, they sampled the supplies, and they trusted their own judgment. It was a reasonable-looking decision made without prayer. The lesson for believers is not that every decision needs a miracle, but that confidence in our own wisdom is dangerous. The people who were sure of themselves were fooled by a few moldy crusts.

The oath they swore becomes binding. Even when the leaders realize they have been deceived, they keep their word. This is a remarkable testimony to the seriousness of vows made in God’s name. Psalm 15:4 describes the person who “swears to his own hurt and does not change.” The Gibeonites are spared, but made servants at the sanctuary. Surprisingly, this turns out for their good. They are brought into the worship of Israel’s God, just as Rahab was. Gibeon would later become a city of the Levites and the site of the tabernacle in Solomon’s time. Out of a deception, God brought mercy.

Chapter 10 shows Israel’s loyalty to a vow. When the five kings attack Gibeon, Joshua could have left the Gibeonites to their fate. They had lied to him. But the oath binds him, so he marches all night. And God honors the faithfulness. The LORD throws hailstones, and the sun and moon pause. Whatever one concludes about the exact nature of this event, the author’s point is plain: this was the LORD fighting for Israel. “There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man.” The statement is stunning. God listens to the prayer of a man. He is not a distant sovereign who ignores his people. He bends to the requests of those who walk in faithfulness.

The chapter also continues the theme of divine warfare. The five kings are brought out, and Joshua has his commanders put their feet on their necks. It is a symbolic act of total victory, and it is an acted parable. The enemies of God’s people will be subdued, and the people share in the victory of their leader. This image will be used again in the New Testament. In Romans 16:20, Paul promises that “the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.” The conquest looks forward to a greater victory.
connection: Joshua’s failure to ask counsel echoes Numbers 27:21, where Joshua was to consult the LORD through Eleazar. The sanctity of oaths is addressed in Numbers 30 and Psalm 15:4. The Gibeonites’ later history appears in 2 Samuel 21:1-9 and 1 Kings 3:4. The hailstones recall the plagues in Exodus 9, and the sun standing still is echoed in Habakkuk 3:11. The feet on the necks of the kings anticipates Psalm 110:1 and 1 Corinthians 15:25.
application:
Make a habit of asking God before you decide. Not only for the big choices, but for the ordinary ones: a commitment, a purchase, a relationship, a job offer. Pause and pray before you say yes. Ask a wise believer to help you see what you might be missing.

Second, take seriously the words you promise. When you give your word, keep it, even when it costs you. A reputation for faithfulness is a witness to the God who keeps his word.

Third, take encouragement from the day the sun stood still. God listens to the prayers of his people. Bring him something that seems too big to ask.

Fourth, see Christ in this story. He saves us when we come to him with nothing, and he brings the deceived and the outsiders near, as he did with Gibeon.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you trust your own judgment without asking God’s.
Ask him to teach you to seek his counsel first and to be someone whose word can be trusted.
Thank him that he fights for his people.
